title: The Aesthetics of Garbage in Philip K. Dick's Martian Time-Slip
author: Ken Simpson

page_summary:
Ken Simpson's 'The Aesthetics of Garbage in Philip K. Dick's Martian Time-Slip' (Canadian Review of American Studies 44.2, Summer 2014, pp. 365–386, University of Toronto Press) is a focused close reading of one novel (Martian Time-Slip, 1964) through the frame of garbage aesthetics in twentieth-century American art and literary culture.

Argument: The proliferation of garbage in Martian Time-Slip is aesthetic, not descriptive or predictive. Simpson develops two structuring principles. First, accumulation of found objects: Dick's trash imagery descends from the Bay Area assemblage artists active during his Point Reyes years (Wallace Berman, Bruce Conner, Wally Hedrick, George Herms, Jess Collins) and from the Beat poets circulating with them. Bruce Conner's The Box (1960) is read alongside Manfred Steiner's 'tomb world' as parallel material instantiations. Second, the sacred grotesque: Dick's trash is not merely degraded but the site of sacred materiality — the divine appearing at the trash stratum, in the inversion of the usual hierarchy of value. The sacred-grotesque frame draws on Bakhtin's Rabelais and on Stam's account of 'redeeming filth.'

The combined frame distinguishes Dick's garbage texts from the later 'palimpsestic' postmodern garbage aesthetics (Don DeLillo's Underworld, the trash motifs in Pynchon) — where postmodern trash registers historical accumulation and the impossibility of disposal, Dick's trash registers the sacred under inversion, and renewal as recovery from the most degraded materials. Simpson positions this as a specifically Dick-era reading: the assemblage artists, the Beats, and PKD share a Bay Area aesthetic of trash-as-revelation that the postmodern frame partly absorbs and partly displaces.

Contributions to PKD studies: (1) the first sustained art-historical reading of PKD's trash motifs against the Bay Area assemblage and Beat lineage that surrounded him geographically and temporally; (2) the sacred-grotesque frame for Dick's garbage that connects his 1960s fiction to his late-period 'divine in the trash stratum' theology (the Exegesis line about coin-operated doors and God); (3) close reading of Manfred Steiner's tomb-world chapters in dialogue with specific assemblage works; (4) integration of Bakhtin and Stam into PKD criticism in a way the field had not previously deployed.

Position in the literature: works against the descriptive-predictive readings of Martian Time-Slip (the novel as anticipating ecological collapse or postcolonial Mars) and in dialogue with Christopher Palmer's tonal-postmodern frame (Exhilaration and Terror, 2003). The sacred-grotesque reading also speaks to J. K. Thomas's 'Coin-Operated Doors and God' (2014) on Ubik — the same year, the same insight that PKD's 'trash stratum' material is theological.
